title: Lends and lexical borrowing
description: Ownership, explicit mut, projections as inline callbacks, law disjoint, and why borrows never escape their block.

exercises.title: Spell the mutation
exercises.prompt: Given fn bump(mut xs: [V]Int, by: Int), which call adds 1 to every element of the caller's array a?
exercises.hint: A mutable borrow is written at both ends: the parameter and the call.
exercises.solution: bump(mut a, 1). The parameter says mut xs and the call says mut a, so every line that can change a visibly contains mut a.
options: bump(a, 1)
bump(a.copy(), 1)
bump(mut a, 1)
bump(&mut a, 1)
exercises.explanation: bump(a, 1) and bump(a.copy(), 1) both omit the required mut and are rejected. An explicit owned copy would not change a anyway. &mut is Rust syntax; CP Lang has no reference operator.
exercises.code:
fn bump(mut xs: [V]Int, by: Int):
    for v in V: xs[v] += by

exercises.title: Why a projection cannot dangle
exercises.prompt: fn at(mut self, i: V) lends mut Int ends with the tail expression mut cnt[i]. Why can the caller never keep a dangling reference to cnt[i]?
exercises.hint: Think about what b.at(v) += 5 desugars to, and where that code runs.
exercises.solution: A projection is sugar for fn at(mut self, i: V, use: (mut Int) -> R) -> R = use(mut cnt[i]), with the callback inlined. The rest of the caller's expression is the callback, it runs while at is still on the stack, and nothing reference-like is ever returned.
options: The caller's expression runs as an inlined callback inside at, so the borrow ends before at returns
The runtime reference-counts every cell of cnt
The checker infers a lifetime parameter for the returned reference
The projection copies cnt[i], so there is no reference at all
exercises.explanation: There is no reference counting and no lifetime inference: the design avoids both. A projection does not copy; b.at(v) += 5 really changes cnt[v], which is the point of a mutable projection.

exercises.title: Prove the law at the call
exercises.prompt: Bag.at declares @law disjoint(i, j) = i != j, and Bag.other is a second projection that also lends cnt[i]. Which call does the checker accept?
exercises.hint: The law only relates two lends of the same projection, and the fact must be visible before the call.
exercises.solution: The guarded call through the same projection. The enclosing if gives the checker i != j, which is exactly the law of at, so the two mutable lends cannot overlap.
options: move(mut b.at(i), mut b.at(j)) with nothing known about i and j
if i != j: move(mut b.at(i), mut b.other(j))
move(mut b.at(i), mut b.at(i)) followed by assert i != j
if i != j: move(mut b.at(i), mut b.at(j))
exercises.explanation: Without the guard nothing proves i != j, so the call is rejected with help to guard or assert. Different projections (at and other) are never assumed disjoint, even when i != j. An assert after the call is too late, and lending b.at(i) twice can never satisfy i != j.

exercises.title: Return the window, not the slice
exercises.prompt: A helper should find the best segment of a, and the caller then sorts that segment in place. Which design fits CP Lang's borrowing rules?
exercises.hint: A slice is a borrow; a range is a plain value.
exercises.solution: Return Range<V> and re-project at the point of use: sort(mut a[w]). The range can be stored, returned, or pushed anywhere, and the borrow is created only where the caller applies it.
options: fn best(a: [V]Int) -> [V]Int returning a[l..=r]
fn best(a: [V]Int) -> Range<V> returning l..=r, then sort(mut a[best(a)])
Store a[l..=r] in a struct field and sort it later
Assign a[l..=r] to a var and return the var
exercises.explanation: Returning a slice, storing it in a field, or assigning it to a var would each let the borrow outlive its block, and the prototype rejects all three with help to keep the range or call .copy(). A copy compiles too, but sorting a copy would not change a.

exercises.title: Predict the boundary prefix sum
exercises.prompt: This prototype-tested program builds prefix sums indexed by boundaries: pre[v.r] = pre[v.l] + a[v]. Predict the output for each input.
exercises.hint: V.last.r is the boundary after the last element, so pre at that boundary covers every element.
exercises.solution: pre starts at 0 everywhere, and each step adds one element to the previous boundary. The final boundary holds the whole sum: 2 - 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, a single -9 gives -9, and three zeros give 0. No +1 index arithmetic is needed because v.l and v.r are boundary values, not shifted integers.

title: Algebra, data structures, and Rooted
description: Bare operators, Monoid(id, op), Action(id, compose, apply, over: op), desc(x), explicit two-pointer windows, and Rooted<V> tree paths.

exercises.title: Predict the fold
exercises.prompt: sum(a) is a fold of + starting from the identity 0. Predict the output of this prototype-tested program for each input.
exercises.hint: Write the fold out as ((0 + x1) + x2) + ..., and remember that adding 0 changes nothing.
exercises.solution: The fold starts at the identity 0 and adds each element: 0 + 5 - 2 + 4 = 7; -3 + 3 = 0; and a single element is just itself, -9, because 0 + x == x.

exercises.title: Which combine can a segment tree use?
exercises.prompt: A segment tree regroups pieces freely. Which combine gives correct range answers however the query splits?
exercises.hint: Check (x op y) op z against x op (y op z) on three small numbers.
exercises.solution: max is associative, max(max(x, y), z) == max(x, max(y, z)), with identity Int.MIN, so it is a monoid and any grouping gives the same answer.
options: (a, b) => max(a, b)
(a, b) => a - b
(a, b) => keep whichever piece was combined first on a tie, else the larger
exercises.explanation: Averaging is not associative: avg(avg(2, 4), 6) = 4.5 but avg(2, avg(4, 6)) = 3.5; carry (sum, count) instead. Subtraction is not associative either. A rule that depends on combination history gives answers that depend on how the query happens to split across nodes.

exercises.title: When two prefix values are enough
exercises.prompt: Which range query can always be answered from two prefix values, prefix(r) combined with the inverse of prefix(l - 1)?
exercises.hint: Taking a prefix back out needs an inverse operation.
exercises.solution: Range sum: + has the inverse -, so sum(l..=r) = pre[r.r] - pre[l.l]. That is why Fenwick<D, Int> is sum-only while arbitrary monoids belong in SegTree.
options: Range maximum
Range minimum
Range gcd
Range sum
exercises.explanation: Maximum, minimum, and gcd have no inverse: knowing max(1..=r) and max(1..=l-1) tells you nothing about max(l..=r). Use SegTree<V, Int>(max, a) or SparseTable<V, Int>(min, a) for those; Fenwick<V, Int>(a) stays dedicated to sums.

exercises.title: Order matters
exercises.prompt: Using the prototype-tested compose_all from this lesson, what does the program print for input 2, then 3 0, then 2 1? Each line is mul add, and the maps apply in order.
exercises.hint: Apply x => 3x first, then x => 2x + 1, and expand.
exercises.solution: First x => 3x, then x => 2(3x) + 1 = 6x + 1, so it prints 6 1. In the opposite order (2 1 then 3 0) the result is 6x + 3: same multiplier, different constant, so the operation is associative but not commutative.
exercises.explanation: 6 3 is the answer for the reversed order, which is the classic mistake of combining a right-hand accumulator in the wrong order. 5 1 adds the multipliers instead of multiplying them.

exercises.title: Bare operators vs. Monoid(id, op)
exercises.prompt: In CP Lang v2.2, how do you construct a range-sum SegTree and a custom (best, count) SegTree over domain V?
exercises.hint: Standard associative operators need no wrapper; custom node combines use Monoid(id, op).
exercises.solution: Pass the bare operator + for range sums (SegTree<V, Int>(+, a)) and Monoid(id, op) for a custom combine over a node value.
options: SegTree<V, Int>(+, a) for sum, and SegTree<V, (Int, Int)>(Monoid(id, op), init) for custom nodes
Wrap + in a custom wrapper struct before passing it to SegTree
Sub-class a SegTree base class and override combine()
Pass a string "+" that SegTree parses at runtime
exercises.explanation: CP Lang v2.2 has no single-purpose operator wrapper types. Built-in associative operators (+, *, ^, &, |, min, max, gcd) pass directly to SegTree and SparseTable, while custom monoids pass Monoid(id, op) and lazy tags pass stock tags like AddSum or Action(id, compose, apply).

exercises.title: What a local library costs
exercises.prompt: A solution uses lib.treap from a large personal library configured in cp.toml (planned). What ends up in the submitted C++?
exercises.hint: Judges accept one file and know nothing about your folders.
exercises.solution: Everything used is inlined into the single submitted C++ file and unused code is removed, so a big library does not bloat submissions. Brutes and laws in the library are stripped too.
options: The whole library folder, concatenated
An include of the library path on your machine
Only the code the solution reaches, inlined into one file and tree-shaken
Nothing until the judge downloads the library
exercises.explanation: Concatenating the folder would waste size and compile time. An include of a local path fails on the judge. Judges never fetch dependencies.

title: Memo, checkers, interactors, and stress testing
description: Recurrences with @memo, slow references with @brute, typed generators and shrinking, multi-answer checkers, query budgets, and first divergence.

exercises.title: Predict the recurrence
exercises.prompt: f(0) = 1 and f(i) = f(i - 1) * 3 + i. Predict the output of this runnable program (which prints f(n - 1)) for each n.
exercises.hint: 0..n is half-open, so the last index is n - 1. Build the values upward from f(0).
exercises.solution: The sequence is f(0) = 1, f(1) = 4, f(2) = 14, f(3) = 45, f(4) = 139, and the program prints f(n - 1). So n = 1 prints 1, n = 3 prints 14, and n = 5 prints 139. A common mistake is treating 0..n as inclusive and printing f(n).

exercises.title: What makes a good brute
exercises.prompt: You suspect range_sum, which uses a prefix table. Which @brute(range_sum) is most useful?
exercises.hint: A brute should be too simple to share the fast version's bug.
exercises.solution: The direct loop. It is obviously correct, it checks exactly the suspect function, and cpl stress shrinks to the first failing case, such as l=1 r=1.
options: A copy of range_sum with different variable names
A brute for the whole program that also uses the prefix table
No brute: compare against the sample output only
sum(a[i] for i in l..=r), a direct loop over the range
exercises.explanation: A renamed copy shares every bug. A whole-program brute built on the same prefix table shares the idea and only says the final answer differs. Samples are a handful of cases, while cpl stress tries thousands of generated inputs and shrinks the first counterexample.

exercises.title: A good shrink step
exercises.prompt: A stress failure has n = 37, twelve queries, and the constraint l <= r on each query. Which step does the planned structure-aware shrinker take?
exercises.hint: Every candidate must stay a valid input and must reproduce the same bug.
exercises.solution: It deletes a query (or an element, or lowers a value) while keeping every constraint true, and accepts the candidate only if it fails at the same first differing stage or crash line.
options: Delete random bytes from the input file
Remove one query, and keep the smaller case only if it still fails the same way
Swap l and r in a query to make the first number smaller
Keep any smaller case that fails for any reason
exercises.explanation: Byte deletion produces invalid input. Swapping l and r can break l <= r. Accepting any failure lets the shrinker drift to a different bug than the one you are chasing.

exercises.title: Who decides existence
exercises.prompt: In the approved @checker design for a print-any-valid-coloring problem, the brute prints -1 because no coloring exists. When does your output pass?
exercises.hint: The checker judges an answer; something else settles whether an answer exists.
exercises.solution: Only -1 passes. The brute settles existence; when it does find an answer, your output must parse as [V]Color and pass valid. The checker never needs to decide whether a coloring exists, which keeps it short.
options: Only when your output is also -1
When valid(c) returns true for your coloring
Whenever your output parses as [V]Color
When your output equals the brute's output character for character
exercises.explanation: Printing a coloring when none exists is wrong, so valid is not even consulted. Parsing is necessary but not sufficient. Character-for-character comparison is exactly what checkers replace.

exercises.title: Fit the query limit
exercises.prompt: An interactive problem has a secret in 1..=1e9 and allows at most 30 queries via ask("?", x, limit: 30) paired with @interactor. Which strategy fits the budget for every secret?
exercises.hint: Count how many halvings it takes to get from 10^9 candidates to one.
exercises.solution: Binary search with bsearch_first(1..=1e9, ok) needs at most 30 asks, because 2^30 is just over 10^9. Locally, @interactor enforces limit: 30 and prints the query transcript if a 31st is made.
options: Ask every value from 1 upward
Ask 30 random values and answer the closest
Binary search with bsearch_first(1..=1e9, ok), about log2(1e9) questions
Ternary search with two asks per step
exercises.explanation: A linear scan needs up to 10^9 asks. Random asks are not correct. Ternary search with two asks per step needs about 2 * log base 1.5 of 10^9, roughly 100, far more than 30.
